https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Maria Shuvalova and her husband have invested in an energy-storage system, in preparation for the arrival of their baby. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Maria Shuvalova and her husband have invested in an energy-storage system, in preparation for the arrival of their baby. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Ukraine Kyiv has become a frontline city - and winter is on the way Residents of Ukraine’s capital prepare for power cuts, drones and bitter cold by stocking up on generators, food and ‘dry showers’ Charlotte Higgins in Kyiv. Photographs by Julia Kochetova Sat 26 Sep 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 03.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I t felt like the last day of summer. On a Sunday afternoon in late September, people in Kyiv strolled through the city’s botanical gardens, admiring the late-flowering dahlias. Later, the terraces in the Podil area – a neighbourhood full of bars, patisseries and bookshops – filled up with customers in search of a cocktail. The idyll was an illusion. As the day darkened, the air defence began its rumble and boom. When a projectile fell with an explosive smack on a bar table, the drinkers flinched and then laughed. It was only a conker from the chestnut tree overhead. Nursing a glass of rosé, writer Myroslav Laiuk talked about the picnic he and his wife had had the previous evening, in a park in the Obolon district – prosecco in proper glasses, cheese and charcuterie. Then a drone was shot down above their heads. Very pretty, he said, with a smile. Shooting stars. Time to make a wish. Kyiv is no longer the city it was in the summer. Since late August, the Russians have been attacking over and over again in daylight hours, rather than only at night. The crump of air-defence, whine of drones and thunder of explosions are no longer the grim music of the night, but a commonplace waking-hours symphony, disrupting schools and workplaces and threatening life. Warehouses and city petrol stations have been targeted, and at times acrid smoke blurs the clear autumn mornings. Kyiv has become a frontline city. And winter is on the way. Winter is something to dread in Kyiv. Last year the cold was terrible – temperatures into the minus 20s – and cruelly long-lasting, persisting well into February. Illustrator Sergiy Maidukov was one of many who lost heating in his flat after the Russians attacked power infrastructure, the invaders’ aim seemingly to make the capital unliveable. The indoor temperature dropped to 3C. He kept warm by layering up, but also by going for runs. View image in fullscreen Daily life in Lukyanivka district of Kyiv – the most damaged neigbourhood by the Russian attacks. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian “At least for 10 minutes afterwards you felt a like normal person, and you could just wear a T-shirt”, he said. He had a steady gas supply, so he could heat up water in a saucepan for a basic wash afterwards. At intervals he’d get up from his work and dance or do push-ups – not an option for the infirm. As film-maker Iryna Tsilyk put it: “Young and strong people – they will survive every time. But how about all those invisible people that we usually don’t meet?” Tsilyk’s biggest fear was, she said, the loss of internet connectivity. Lack of water supply would be another nightmare. Maria Shuvalova, an editor in academic publishing, described the period two winters ago when, for several days, the water supply failed both in her flat and in her coworking space. She was drinking tea to keep warm while working, then needing the loo. So she would walk the 20 minutes home, pee in a bottle, then return to the coworking space; then drink more tea, and repeat the whole cycle. For bowel movements, there was a plastic bag, knotted and disposed of in the trash. Such details of life were, she joked, “shit you definitely don’t want to know”. View image in fullscreen Food supplies prepared for winter at Maria Shuvalova’s home. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian On a stroll in the botanical gardens, Iryna Gorlach, an international cooperation expert, laughed when asked how she was preparing for the coming cold. She pulled out her phone and showed an Instagram post from a popular Kyiv account. “This winter will be super difficult, we need to prepare properly,” it said. Then three bullet points: “Buy a house in a village; go abroad; stock up on grains and cereals.” Beneath, were the words, “How I’m preparing” and a cartoon image of a panicked-looking dog holding a cross and a copy of the Bible. Leaving the city is certainly on many people’s minds – if only for a few weeks ata time if things get bad. Nastya Dyakova, chief executive of an online safety charity, has rented a seven-bedroom house in the Carpathian mountains, in far western Ukraine , where staff and their families will be able to stay rent free if the situation in Kyiv becomes practically or psychologically untenable. “It is not only a question about winter in Kyiv, but about drones,” she said. Since August, the capital has been assailed by new, faster, jet-powered, harder-to-intercept drones. “It’s become really emotionally challenging to stay in Kyiv, and we understood that it’s difficult for our team to work or to focus because they really worry about their safety. So this option in the Carpathians is available for the next six months, until the end of winter.” View image in fullscreen Halyna is selling flowers next to the burnt market in Lukyanivka district of Kyiv. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian The Lukyanivka neighbourhood of central Kyiv has been particularly hard hit this year, with its huge shopping complex and market bombed out and burned in the early summer. Market traders have set up their stalls beside the ruins anyway: one lady, cheerfully presiding over slabs of salo , pork lard, proclaimed that her personal coping mechanism was going to be a plentiful supply of home distilled hooch or horilka . Another stallholder, Halyna, cheerfully selling bouquets of lavender, dahlias and chrysanthemums, was similarly fatalistic. “It will be whatever God sends us,” she said. View image in fullscreen Viktoriia Riabchenko in Lukyanivka district of Kyiv. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Passing the market en route to work was Viktoriia Riabchenko, an accountant. There had been a particularly good harvest this year in her dacha garden, she said, and she had a great stock of ferments: plums, sour cherries, raspberries, tomatoes, cucumbers and sweet peppers. Not that she was especially concerned about the possibility of food shortages if warehouse bombing continued, she said; Russian propaganda exaggerated the potential problem, and specific shortfalls in shops tended to be remedied fast. View image in fullscreen Viktor, a delivery courier originally from Kramatorsk. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Attitudes to winter, of course, depend on one’s perspective and experience. Viktor, a delivery driver was pausing outside Lukyankivka’s branch of MacDonald’s. The plastic golden arches on the side of the building have lately been restored to crispness after the heat from the summer’s bombs and fires slid them into a Dali-like melt. He was used to the cold, outdoors all day on his moped, and, having moved from Kramatorsk in the Donetsk region, had plenty of experience with bangs and explosions. Ivan Onyshchenko, who had dropped by for a hamburger and fries from his nearby workplace, had invested in a generator that he put on his balcony on the fifth floor – a lot of fuel to carry upstairs if the electricity stayed out. Usually generators chug away at high volume; his, he promised, was “only as loud as a hairdryer”. View image in fullscreen Ivan Onyshchenko at McDonald’s in Lukyanivka district of Kyiv. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Shuvalova lives on the 14th floor of her apartment building, and joked that last year she got great thighs walking up the stairs during power outages. This year will be different though: she and her husband, who is serving in the army, are expecting a baby, and preparing for the winter has been detailed and intense. The couple have plans A, B and C – plan A is to stay in Kyiv, but leaving to stay with friends or family further from the Russian missiles is on the table. Realising they could not expect the baby to live “like moles” as they did last year – reading by candlelight and working by laptop-screen glow during days-long outages – they have invested in an energy-storage system. The unit is in effect a giant battery, about the size of a small carry-on suitcase, that can keep appliances going for a day or so, if need be. Last winter they were on sale for 160,000 UAH (about £2, 700). Cannily, the couple bought one for about half that during the summer. Shuvalova also opened a drawer to reveal an array of small power banks. View image in fullscreen Dry shower packages prepared for winter at Maria’s Shuvalova home. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian The residents of their apartment block are voting on taking over the running of their own building. If they manage it, they will install a generator to power one of the lifts during power cuts, and a toilet for the bomb shelter – AKA the underground car park. Shuvalova opened cupboards to reveal stashes of water, dried grains, rice, and tinned meat. They have a camping stove and a box full of “dry shower” packs – wipes that, with 50ml of water added, can be used to wash. In her anti-natal classes, a lot of emphasis is put on breastfeeding, she said. Formula requires clean water and the ability to heat it – not to be taken for granted this winter. “Breastfeeding takes care of all that,” she said. The air-defence roared away as she spoke. People outside Ukraine may question the decision to have a baby in Kyiv under such circumstances. “We couldn’t postpone any more so we just have to adapt,” said Shuvalova. “It’s bringing a lot of meaning to our life, and joy. And pregnancy hormones are very nice. I’m so calm and not stressing at all.” View image in fullscreen The Lukyanivka neighbourhood has been particularly hard hit this year, with its huge shopping complex and market bombed out and burned in the early summer. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Whether fatalistic, downhearted, or meticulously prepared, the boundaries of “acceptable” or “ordinary” have been pushed outwards for Kyivans in ways unimaginable to the inhabitants of other European capitals. Only one thing is absolutely certain this unpredictable, dreaded coming winter: that it will end. According to Maidukov, the illustrator, “In the evening when you are already blue and trembling, you’re thinking, ‘OK, one day is behind me, and I need to bear maybe two or three more weeks of this, which is not such a long time’.” Last winter’s freeze, he said, was a “weird period. Each day I was on the edge, about to fall down with my morale, but I didn’t allow myself to. Because nothing will stop spring. Spring will definitely come.” Explore more on these topics Ukraine Europe Russia features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m2.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The discovery of 12 bodies in an area east of Johannesburg has sparked alarm in South Africa By Khanyisile Ngcobo Reporting from Johannesburg Published 28 September 2026 Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of the bodies of three more women in an area east of Johannesburg, bringing the total number of bodies found there to 12 in just two months. The latest bodies were found in Ekurhuleni between Saturday and Monday morning, according to local police. Police have made arrests in three of the cases, which do not appear to be related to the others. Nevertheless, police have said they cannot rule out the possibility of a serial killer. The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concerns about high levels of violence against women in South Africa. Here's what we know. Busisiwe Mahlangu Case 1 Busisiwe Mahlangu's body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July 2026, the first of a string of bodies found in Ekurhuleni within a two-month period. The 37-year-old was found naked with her hands bound with cable ties. Police arrested a suspect, believed to be her partner, two days after her murder. He has been in police custody since then and has not been linked to the other deaths that followed. Itumeleng Kekana Image source, Kekana family Case 2 Itumeleng Kekana, 32, was the second woman whose body was found in the same area on 3 August 2026. The young mother disappeared in July and her body was found badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge in Kempton Park. No arrests have been made so far. Nomfesane Mjobo Case 3 Nomfesane Mjobo's body was found on 26 August, also in Kempton Park. Few details around her death have been released but like most of the victims, she was found partially or fully naked with bruises. No arrests have been made. Unknown woman Case 4 Police confirmed the discovery of an unknown woman, in her 20s, on 7 September. The woman's body was found floating in a river in Olifantsfontain wearing only her underwear. No further details have been shared about her death and no arrests have been made. Gracious Nkomo Image source, South African police Case 5 Gracious Nkomo was the fifth woman whose body was discovered, again in the Kempton Park area. Her partially clothed body was found on 10 September along a road close to South Africa's busiest airport. No arrests have been made in the 28-year-old's death. Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBC Case 6 Elizabeth Moselakgomo was the sixth woman to be found, after a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for a daily run near her home in Kempton Park. Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. It was the discovery of her body that really raised the alarm about the spate of killings. No arrests have been made in her case. Figure caption, Women held a memorial run in Johannesburg after the discovery of Moselakgomo's body Unidentified woman Case 7 Police confirmed the discovery of another body just two days after Moselakgomo was found. The body was found in Olifantsfontein on 14 September, but police have withheld her name as her family has not yet been informed. No arrests have been made. Dineo Motapane Image source, Dineo Motapane Case 8 The body of Dineo Motapane, 38, was discovered on 15 September just two days after she was last seen alive. Motapane's battered and partly burned body was found on the side of the road in Springs, another part of Ekurhuleni. She leaves behind a young child. No arrests have been made in her case. Jabulile Ntimba Case 9 The body of Jabulile Ntimba, in her 30s, was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. This was the ninth body found in Ekurhuleni. According to police, it appears Ntimba was killed because of a possible love triangle. Three people, two women and a man, were initially arrested for her grisly murder but the man was released due to insufficient evidence. The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice. Ntombifuthi Nxumalo Case 10 The body of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, the 10th body found in Ekurhuleni, was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body. This has led to police believing she may have been stoned to death. A 36-year-old man was arrested a day after Nxumalo's death after he had travelled to another province. He faces a murder charge. Unidentified woman Case 11 The body of a yet-to-be identified woman was found in Springs on Sunday - the 11th body found in Ekurhuleni. The grim discovery was made by a security company patrolling the area. The woman was found in an open field, but no further details have been shared. No arrests have been made. Boitumelo Gift Mashita Case 12 Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken. Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand. Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies. While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September. The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg. It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni. President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience". South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone. South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day. Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; Â£18,000) for information that could lead to arrests. https://dailypioneer.com/news/romania-pr.text: September 18, 2026 Romania's president nominates Siegfried Muresan as new PM to break deadlock Copy Link X WhatsApp Share By Associated Press Source: X/@SMuresan Romanian President Nicusor Dan nominated Liberal European lawmaker Siegfried Muresan on Thursday to be prime minister as he seeks to end a months-long political crisis after his previous two picks failed. Dan nominated the 44-year-old member of the European Parliament and the centre-right National Liberal Party, or PNL, to try to form a government. Dan made two nominations in June after a no-confidence vote toppled Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan in May. “We are more than four months after the government was dismissed … and during this period, we have had hundreds of hours of discussions, both together and separately, with political parties to find a solution to this crisis,” Dan said at the presidential Cotroceni Palace in the capital, Bucharest. “Romania needs a government.” “I chose to designate for the position of prime minister the person who has the most votes cast today by the parties in the consultations today. This person is Siegfried Muresan,” he added. “We do not have a clear majority, despite all these hours of discussions.” Shortly after his nomination, Muresan said in a Facebook post, “I accept the proposal made by the president of Romania.” Dan said Muresan's experience in the European Parliament qualifies him for the premiership. Muresan became an MEP in 2014, and is vice chair of the European People's Party group in the European Parliament. Muresan has 10 days to present a cabinet to Parliament. When the previous coalition came to power in June 2025, its priority was to reduce the budget deficit, but Bolojan found himself frequently at loggerheads with PSD over austerity measures. Bolojan was sworn in with the aim of ending one of Romania's worst political crises in its post-Communist history but was ousted after a motion was submitted by the PSD, which was part of the coalition, and the nationalist opposition Alliance for the Unity of Romanians party. He has remained prime minister in an interim capacity since. Sorin Grindeanu, leader of the opposition Social Democratic Party, or PSD, said Thursday that he noted with “surprise and disappointment” Dan's nomination and that he had convened his party's National Permanent Bureau for a meeting on Monday to “carefully analyse” the proposal. “It is difficult to understand the reasoning behind the head of state's choice of someone like Muresan,” he said in a Facebook post. “Romania, however, finds itself in an extremely difficult situation.” Between 2000 and 2004, Muresan studied at Bucharest's Academy of Economic Studies, and then took a Master's program in Economics and Management Science at Humboldt University in Berlin. Before becoming an MEP, he was an adviser to the EPP. Dan had previously nominated Adrian Vestea for the premiership, but his proposal for a government was rejected by Parliament. Before him, Eugen Tomac withdrew before a vote in Parliament. Cristian Andrei, a Bucharest-based political consultant, says there is little chance Muresan's nomination will lead to a majority among Romania's pro-European parties and that he expects “further political stalemate.” “The centre-right coalition around Muresan has very little chance to win the support of the Parliament,” he told The Associated Press. “But it also opens the door for a future collaboration between the Social Democrats and the populists. … The president is putting blame on the political parties for not being able to create such a majority.” The prime ministerial position was set to be rotated in 2027 from Bolojan to a PSD premier as part of a power-sharing agreement. https://www.theguardian.com/community/li.text: Clifford Weiler, San Diego, CA asks in a callout question: Politicians cite how the economy is improving, but how is the rising rate of inflation taken into account? Lauren: What growth in the economy means really depends on who you’re talking to. For economists, economic growth is measured by gross domestic product (GDP), which is an equation adding together consumption, investment, government spending and net exports. A little inflation can actually stimulate further growth, as long as it doesn’t lead to a pullback in spending. That’s why the US Federal Reserve’s target inflation rate is 2% (something that hasn’t been seen since January 2021 – for context, it was 3.7% in September). For both economists and politicians, inflation really only becomes a bad thing when it starts to impact consumer spending. https://www.ttnworldwide.com:443/Article.text: Travel, Tourism & Hospitality Pegasus Airlines completes acquisition of Czech Airlines, Smartwings October 2026 Share Pegasus Airlines has completed its acquisition of Czech Airlines and the Smartwings Group after receiving all required regulatory approvals and meeting customary closing conditions, marking a major step in the Turkish carrier’s international expansion. The transaction brings together two established aviation businesses with complementary strengths and a combined fleet of more than 175 aircraft. The airlines also have firm orders for 140 additional aircraft, providing significant potential for future growth. Founded in 1990, Pegasus adopted its low-cost business model in 2005 and now serves 161 destinations across 57 countries. The airline operates one of the world’s youngest and most fuel-efficient fleets. Smartwings Group, together with the Czech Airlines brand, is one of Central and Eastern Europe’s longstanding airline groups. It serves 80 destinations across 20 countries and maintains strong relationships with major tour operators, particularly in the leisure travel market. Under the new partnership, Pegasus and Smartwings aim to strengthen competitiveness while combining Pegasus’ international network, operational expertise and low-cost model with Smartwings’ established regional presence. Smartwings will continue operating under the Smartwings and Czech Airlines brands, maintaining existing operations, customer relationships and service delivery. The companies said the partnership will support innovation, development and talent, while focusing on safety, operational excellence and customer experience as they expand connectivity across Europe and beyond. Güliz Öztürk, CEO of Pegasus Airlines, said: “Our story began with a dream of a world where everyone can fly, and today, Pegasus Airlines and Smartwings come together to take that ambition forward. Together we can grow further and offer our guests more choice than any of us could alone. The people and relationships behind each airline are the reason I'm confident in what comes next, and we look forward to writing the next chapter together with all our colleagues.” Jiří Šimáně, Co-founder of Smartwings, added:“Smartwings has been built over many years by dedicated people and by the loyalty of passengers and partners, to whom I am deeply grateful. We are confident that Pegasus Airlines is the right partner to build on these strengths, support future growth and create lasting value for everyone connected with both airlines.” -TTN RELATED STORIES
